transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-30
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Rory Patel (Redwood SE), Jason Lee (Redwood SE), Sophia Klein (Alpen Head Eng), Liam Park (Alpen ML Infra), Ivy Torres (Alpen CTO), Marco Ruiz (Alpen PM)

Summary: Quick 'lab' style walkthrough of Redwood Optimize recommendations — focusing on prefetch/prefix KV cache plus batching guidance for Alpen's commerce assistant workload. High-level buy-in from Alpen; asked for concrete configs + trial Dedicated cluster for benchmarks.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for taking time, quick roll call, i know we got Ivy on the call, Sophia, Liam, Marco, thanks for joining. we wanted to run a hands-on lab today and map your traffic profile to batching + prefetch recommendations and show the console cost simulator, is that still the ask?
[00:12] Sophia: yeah that's right, thanks Maya. main thing for us is reduce per-conversation costs while keeping p95 < 250ms for our live assistant. we're also  concerned about data residency for europe customers - want to make sure prefetch doesn't leak anything.
[00:25] Ivy: and timeline— we want to have a pilot in prod in ~6 weeks if numbers look good.
[00:30] Maya: perfect. rory and jason from my side will do the technical bits. rory do you want to frame the cost model quickly and then we can map to alpen's profile?
[00:38] Rory: yeah sure. high level: cost model inputs are tokens per request, average response tokens, concurrency, target p95 latency, and cache hit rate. Redwood Optimize simulates batching effect on per-token GPU amortization and the marginal cost saved via prefix/KV prefetch. we assume typical transformer throughput curves — smaller batches reduce efficiency but improve latency.
[00:58] Marco: quick question — we have a mix of short Q/A and long-form summaries. can the prefetch help both?
[01:05] Rory: depends. prefix prefetch works best when the conversation context is re-used across turns or when you can warm the KV cache (for example, long-running sessions where the first token is often the same). for one-off long generative responses, batching is the main lever.
[01:22] Lily: sorry who said lily? (crosstalk)
[01:25] Maya: oh ignore, that's my slack ping.
[01:28] Liam: concrete numbers — our current prod profile: median prompt tokens ~40, median response tokens ~120, peak concurrent requests ~600, average QPS ~1200 across regions, p95 latency target 250ms, SLO 99.5.
[01:42] Rory: good, that tells us a lot. run that through the simulator, for your 1.2k QPS profile with ~120 response tokens, naive hosted single-request pattern yields fairly high per-token cost because throughput per GPU is low. when you allow batching you can increase throughput by packing concurrent requests; the simulator shows cost drops sharply once you get to average batch sizes of 8-12 for your token lengths.
[02:03] Ivy: is that inside our latency budget? p95 250ms is tight.
[02:07] Rory: yes if we keep batching windows small and prioritize latency buckets. Redwood supports adaptive batching — meaning we set a maximum batching window (e.g., 40ms) and a max batch size. for your traffic, with a 40ms window we saw p95 impacts in the 10-20ms range; the baseline token emission dominates.
[02:25] Jason: i'll share the console chart — (screen share noises) — this is the cost-sim view, x-axis is average batch size, y-axis is $/k tokens. you can toggle prefetch hit rate. see how the curve flattens after batch size ~12.
[02:40] Marco: ok so to hit cost target we need to accept a small batching window. what's the tradeoff if we go to dedicated?
[02:46] Rory: dedicated capacity buys you predictability and lower unit costs at scale — you remove multi-tenant overhead and can use different kernel/quantization profiles. for example, a Dedicated 2x8 cluster at your concurrency can cut unit cost roughly 25-40% in the sim depending on batch utilization. but there's commit/ops overhead.
[03:03] Sophia: and prefetch — how does KV prefetch interact with sessionization? what's our best pattern?
[03:09] Rory: two common patterns: session-cache (pin a session to a worker and keep KV around) or prefix prefetch (proactively fetch likely KV entries before the full request). session-cache is great for long-lived sessions with a single user; prefix prefetch is great when you have many short sessions that share a common prefix or system prompt. your commerce assistant has a mix — product recommended flows reuse product info across turns; that is ripe for prefix prefetch.
[03:35] Liam: our session TTL today is 10 minutes, but many sessions are 30-60s. does prefetch add memory pressure?
[03:41] Rory: yes memory and ingress. Optimize's sim factors in TTL and average entry size. if your prefetch hit rate is high, you save compute but increase memory. we recommended tuning TTL to match session lifetime distribution; in practice we saw best results with TTL in the 2-5 minute range for high-churn chat, and longer for authenticated multi-turn flows.
[03:58] [04:00] Jason: quick demo — i'm going to flip to the console 'prefetch planner' sheet and upload a sample traffic file. (typing) here's the traffic histogram for an evening peak — you can see microbursts that will help batching reuse.
[04:16] Marco: those microbursts are from cart-abandonment flows — high concurrency for ~3-8s windows.
[04:20] Rory: those are perfect for ephemeral batch packing — we typically recommend enabling adaptive batching with a short window during microbursts to grab more requests into each GPU batch without penalizing p95 much.
[04:33] Sophia: can we do a conservative prefetch to avoid incorrect cached history? we can't surface stale product inventory data.
[04:39] Maya: that's a good callout. Redwood's prefetch can be coupled to TTLs and validation hooks. you can set a lookahead that fetches read-only context but have a short TTL, and also tag cache entries as 'volatile' so the console will bias against using stale entries for inventory-sensitive fields.
[04:55] Ivy: regarding compliance — we need SOC2 + encryption at rest and KMS control. any prefetch data stored in KV will fall under our data residency rules?
[05:05] Maya: yes. on Hosted we separate by region and store KV entries within the same region. for Private/VPC deployments you control the KMS and material; for Dedicated we can enable customer-managed KMS. all KV metadata is logged to audit events.
[05:19] Liam: perfect. do you have any numbers for hit-rate sensitivity? like going from 10% to 40% hit rate how much cost savings?
[05:26] Rory: absolutely — with your token profile, going from 10% to 40% prefix hit rate reduces per-response compute by approx 18-28% in the sim (because cache hits avoid full attention passes and reduce token expansion). combined with batching it compounds — we can model that in the spreadsheet.
[05:44] Marco: is there a recommended rollout pattern? we don't want to flip a switch and break things.
[05:49] Rory: canary strategy: start with a small percentage of traffic (5-10%) enabling prefix prefetch and a conservative TTL; run for 48 hours, validate correctness and latency, then incremental ramp. Redwood Console supports canary metrics and automatic rollback if quality/regression triggers fire.
[06:03] Sophia: what about cold starts? first request the cache miss will add latency, right?
[06:07] Rory: yes a miss can add a small prefetch overhead if you chose synchronous prefetch. We encourage async prefetch in many cases: prefetch likely keys in background after request arrival so that subsequent turns are warm. that requires you instrument events to trigger prefetch candidates.
[06:19] Ivy: instrument events — meaning our prod side would call a Redwood prefetch endpoint? we prefer not to add extra network hops.
[06:25] Maya: you can either emit lightweight events to Redwood or let the Redwood runtime infer candidates from incoming prompts (we call that console-driven heuristics). both work; for low-latency infra we usually use heuristics with webhook verification.
[06:37] Liam: ok let's get concrete — show us a recommended config for our profile.
[06:41] Jason: pulling up the exported recommendation... (typing) suggested baseline: adaptive batching window 40ms, max batch size 16, prefix prefetch enabled for product-context keys, TTL 180s for product context, TTL 30s for volatile inventory keys, session affinity for authenticated users with sessionization TTL 10m, prefetch concurrent workers 4.
[07:01] Sophia: sounds reasonable — curious about memory footprint for TTL 180s across 1.2k QPS.
[07:07] Rory: rough calc — average key size ~2KB, 40% hit rate, average live entries at any time ~QPS * session_lifetime * hit_rate adjustment... translate that: with your hist we see ~60-120GB of memory footprint on a Dedicated cluster, which is well within a 2x-GPU host pool. we'll detail this in the spreadsheet.
[07:28] Marco: does the console give a line-item for memory vs compute cost?
[07:32] Jason: yes — cost simulator splits into compute (GPU hours), memory $ (if Dedicated) and ingress/egress where relevant. also we model wasted prefetch traffic vs realized hits.
[07:43] Sophia: ok, what about eviction policy? LRU? time-based?
[07:46] Rory: default is TTL + size-based eviction; you can opt into LRU heuristics. for predictable caches we often prefer GCRA style TTL with occasional LRU to trim hot-but-stale entries.
[07:57] Ivy: security quick Q — is the cache encrypted at rest and do we have key rotation?
[08:02] Maya: yes — AWS KMS rotation or customer-managed HSM for Private. we also log all reads for audit — you can configure masking rules.
[08:12] Liam: any integration with our existing secret manager?
[08:15] Maya: yes we can integrate with vault/AWS secrets manager for credentials and the console supports SSO SAML for access control and role-based permissions for who can alter TTLs.
[08:26] Marco: peoples question: competition — if we self-host we have more control, why choose Redwood?
[08:31] Rory: self-hosting gives control but costs engineering time and ops. Redwood gives you the runtime optimizations (kernel selection, batching, prefix prefetch integration) and the console for cost/quality tradeoffs with less build/ops. also we have fallbacks and rollout tooling to minimize regressions.
[08:49] Sophia: okay can we run a quick sim with a 40% prefetch hit and 10ms allowed batching window?
[08:56] Jason: doing it now. (typing) result: at 40% hit, 10ms window — cost drop is ~12% vs baseline but p95 increases by ~18ms. at 40ms window cost drop is ~25% and p95 increases by ~22ms; both within your target.
[09:17] Marco: so 40ms seems better for cost but similar p95. why is 10ms p95 better but less saving?
[09:23] Rory: because smaller window captures fewer concurrent requests, so you're not amortizing GPU startup and underutilize kernel throughput.
[09:29] Ivy: we like the sound of a 40ms window if p95 stays <250.
[09:33] Maya: noted. next, on instrumentation — what telemetry do you need us to provide for the deeper run?
[09:39] Liam: we'd export request traces, token counts per request, and routing breakdown. also we'd prefer a small synthetic load for evening peak.
[09:46] Maya: good. we'll give a packet with required formats. we'll also provide a template CSV for the console upload.
[09:52] Sophia: are there any gotchas with function/tool calling and caching? we use tools for price lookups and inventory.
[09:58] Rory: key consideration — don't cache tool outputs that are time-sensitive. treat tool responses as volatile and set TTL=0 or have a validation hook. Redwood supports tool-aware cache tagging.
[10:10] Jason: (shares a short doc link) i'll drop the link to the 'tool-aware caching' design in the follow-up.
[10:14] Marco: what about regression detection — how do we ensure prefetch doesn't reduce quality?
[10:18] Rory: Redwood Console can run automated quality checks against truth prompts; we integrate with your evals or run a shadow traffic comparison during canary. thresholds can be set to auto-roll back.
[10:29] Sophia: okay would like to see a sample config that we can hand to our infra for a test.
[10:33] Rory: will do. I'll include sample YAML for the runtime and a sandbox harness for the trial.
[10:38] Ivy: cost contracts — if we go Dedicated what's the minimum commit?
[10:42] Maya: Dedicated minimums vary by region, but typical entry is monthly reserved capacity with a 3-month minimum for small pilots. we'll include a pricing sketch.
[10:51] Liam: for the trial we prefer a short 2-week Dedicated eval that we can scale down after the benchmark — is that possible?
[10:56] Maya: usually yes, we can set a trial with limited commit for a narrow window; our Finance & Sales ops will confirm via the follow-up.
[11:03] Marco: let's talk failure modes — what happens if the cache node dies mid-session?
[11:07] Rory: runtime will fallback to serverless hosting pattern for those sessions; clients won't see catastrophic failures but latency will spike for affected requests. Redwood offers automatic fallback policies and retries to maintain availability.
[11:18] Sophia: okay perfect. any quick wins we can run immediately without infra changes?
[11:22] Rory: yes — enable adaptive batching with a conservative window and enable async prefix prefetch heuristics via the console (no extra infra). that alone often yields 8-15% cost savings.
[11:33] Maya: great. i'm going to recap the next steps.
[11:36] Maya: action items — i'll send the cost simulator + console walkthrough recording; rory creates the YAML examples and prefix config; liam will export traffic hist and baseline p95; we'll schedule the 2hr deep dive. any objections?
[11:48] Ivy: none from me. thanks all.
[11:51] Sophia: good session, thanks.
[11:54] Maya: thanks everyone. we'll follow up via email.

End of meeting.
